subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a short statement to make about old age security. The government, and I am sure all hon. members of the house, have read with great interest the proceedings of the joint committee on the Canada pension plan, and I would like if I may, Mr. Speaker, to take this opportunity of congratulating the joint chairmen and the representatives of all parties who were members of the committee. I think I speak for all members of the house when I express appreciation for their work, most of which was done during the recess.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
In reviewing the representations made to the committee, its discussions and its report, the government has come to the conclusion that there should be certain amendments on the lines recommended by the committee, though not identical in all respects, and there is also one major change that should be made in Bill No. C-136 consequent upon the work of the committee. Many of the representations made to the committee were concerned not with the new earnings-related pension as such but with the flat rate pension which is now provided at age 70 for virtually all Canadians under the Old Age Security Act. Some of the proposals put forward are ones that everyone would like to act on, but they are too expensive for the government to accept as financially responsible at this time when there are so many other things that we in Canada need to do.
One of the most urgent of our social needs, however, is to make pensions available at age 65. Bill No. C-136 proposes to do this, over a five year transition period, both for the new earnings-related pension and the flat rate old age security pension. Under the bill as it is now before the house old age security would be paid in a reduced amount the earlier it is taken. Many of the people and organizations submitting briefs to the committee pointed to hardships that this reduction could involve. After reviewing such representations the government has come to the view that it should recommend to parliament that old age security be paid in the full amount from the time people are 65.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That amount at present is, of course, $75, to which it was raised in 1963. Under Bill No. C-136 the $75 will in future increase automatically if the cost of living rises. The additional change the government now recommends is that, beginning next January, the full pension will be paid to people who have reached age 69; the following year the full pension will be paid at age 68, and so on until by 1970 everyone reaching age 65 will be entitled to the full amount of $75 or more, in addition of course to the Canada pension plan benefits which will then be available to newly retiring people.
The government will move this amendment to Bill No. C-136 when the relevant sections in part IV are reached in committee. Since additional expenditures are involved, I hereby give notice of the necessary resolution, in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, which might be taken to the table now, Mr. Speaker. I should make it plain that the old age security pension at age 65

Canada Pension Legislation will not be subject to any retirement or means test.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Old age security is a universal, flat rate benefit, and we do not believe that conditions should be applied in a federal program of this kind. At the same time, however, the government does think it reasonable to recognize that the needs of people between 65 and 70, when many are retired but some are not, vary a great deal. It is therefore the government's intention to recommend to parliament that the Income Tax Act be modified so that the additional personal deduction of $500, now available from age 65, will in future begin at age 70.
This change will, of course, be made only in stages as the old age security benefit becomes available to people at ages earlier than 70. The withdrawal of the additional deduction will not affect people who have little or no income apart from old age security. It will affect only those people between the ages of 65 and 70 who have other resources sufficient to put them into a taxable category.
What is now proposed, Mr. Speaker, will of course cost money. We believe, however, that this cost can and should be met. Through the conjunction of old age security and the Canada pension plan we will have a pension system that puts Canadian social justice in the forefront of achievement throughout the world.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this party I want to express our very warm appreciation of the announcement made today by the Prime Minister. Even though I might wish that the announcement had gone further, what has been announced indicates the value of the work which was done by the joint committee on Bill No. C-136.
I want most of all to say that what is being proposed in this announcement does establish a very important principle, namely that the flat rate old age security pension should be available without a means test at ages below 70. I wish the full pension could start at 65 right away, but at any rate the principle has been established that we are to get down to 65 as the universal age for the paying of pensions under the Old Age Security Act.
With regard to the principle, I wish only to say that it is good and that it is warmly welcomed. In my view the government has done well to pay attention to some of the arguments which were put forward in the joint committee, particularly with respect to the earlier proposal of the government to pay old age security at ages between 65 and 70 at a reduced rate. The government has now come to the realization that that is not a good idea but that instead we are going to have the full amount of the old age security payable at these lower ages. I must say that I wish the progress could be a little swifter in getting down to the age of 65, but at least we are getting it started.
I hope that even yet the government will study the other phases of the work of the joint committee and will note that there was very strong support in the committee not only for lowering the eligible age for old age security but for increasing the amount of the pension under that act. While it is true that my amendment to raise the pension to $100 per month did not receive the support of the committee, there was support for raising it by some amount.
I remind the government that when it brought in the first version of the Canada pension plan in 1963 it recognized that coincident with the Canada pension plan there had to be an increase in the amount of old age security. That increase was brought in separately in 1963, but I submit that when the Canada pension plan benefits begin to be

received by Canadian citizens in 1967, it will not be good enough to leave the fiat rate old age security benefit at $75 per month. Just as the government has now made an announcement as to what is going to happen in 1966, 1967, 1968, 1969 and 1970, I think it should make an announcement as to its intentions for increasing the basic amount of old age security. It is still my view, and the view of this party which has backed me in the move I made in the committee, that the pension ought to be $100 per month payable at age 65.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the announcement that has been made, and we are particularly glad that an important principle has been established, namely that the flat rate universal pension is to be paid to Canadians at age 65.
I have just one other comment to make. I noticed the suggestion of the Prime Minister that the $500 extra exemption on income tax, which is now available to persons age 65 and over, is to be removed progressively. I gained the impression that it is to be removed one year at a time. May I suggest to the government that there is still time to deal with this suggestion, and that if the government feels that with these pensions being paid at these ages it is not necessary to have the differentiation that existed, rather than take away the $500 extra exemption from those over 65 it would be better to increase the exemption for everyone to at least $1,500 under the Income Tax Act. I think that is the kind of change which ought to be considered by the Minister of Finance when he brings down his budget.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members are well aware of the improvements we should like to have made, and I hope I have set them out clearly in the few remarks I have made to the house. But even if there is some suggestion of criticism, and a clear suggestion that something more should be done, on behalf of this party and on behalf of the Canadian people I would state that we welcome the kind of announcement which has been made today.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group I should like to say at once that we are very happy the government has seen fit to bend its ear and pay attention to the proceedings of the Canada pension plan committee, which did work hard to produce results. I was interested in the announcement by the government to the effect that the gap between ages 65 and 70 will be filled. I refer to that gap as the time between the
Canada Pension Legislation normal retirement age of 65 and the eligible age for old age security at 70. We are very happy that this gap is being closed, and we should like to commend the government in this regard.
Mr. Speaker, I am very much concerned about the indexing or tying of the pensions to the cost of living. I am not suggesting that an increase is not needed, but I do think a periodical review is a much superior system to indexing, because by indexing we are opening a door which is tantamount to the lid of Pandora's box. I think we will find ourselves being pressured into indexing for many other purposes with the result of a lessening of the bands on inflation. I think the government should take a very serious look at this situation. If we were to make a proper analysis at this time of the cost of an increase in the amount of old age security payments I think we would find that the overall cost to the Canadian people would not be nearly as great as it might appear on the surface, because if you give the people of Canada something as of right you remove the necessity to give them something because they happen to be unfortunate and in need.
I certainly hope the government may see fit to increase the old age security payment substantially over the amount now paid because, as I have said, I do not think it will cost the taxpayers too much.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO CANADA PENSION LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) state in the house that he intends to become more and more creditist between now and 1970, when he announced that in 1970, old age pensions will be paid without any means test, mind you, to every person aged 65 and over.
Now, this is precisely what the Ralliement Creditiste advocated during the 1962 and 1963 election campaigns. At that time, the Liberals, who are now trying to interrupt me, were afraid of inflation. But when such a suggestion comes from the Prime Minister of Canada, undoubtedly, inflation is no longer a danger.
Mr. Speaker, we are all for the payment of a monthly pension of $75 at age 65, but as pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), what are we going to do about our older citizens until 1970?
At that time pensions of $75 a month will no longer be sufficient. Why not provide immediately for such an old age pension for

Introduction of Legislation the benefit of those who are 65 or older. In addition, people who have reached the age of 60 and who are in need could, after investigation if you wish, be given a similar pension which would enable them to live or at least to survive in their country, Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Prime Minister to the effect that such a pension will be paid in 1970 is nothing but window dressing. Tonight, some old people will feel pretty good when they hear on television the news that they are to get a pension of $75 a month at the age of 65. However, it will not be before they are 69 that they will be entitled to a pension of $75 a month.
At any rate, the pension of $75 a month announced by the Prime Minister and payable at the age of 65, starting in 1970, will no longer be sufficient at that time. I am sure that before 1970 we will have to consider the possibility of providing a pension of $100 a month for all Canadians who are 60 or over.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, we shall support Bill No. C-136, amended as the Prime Minister just announced. Still, we feel that that is too little and that it is merely window dressing. The government will have to introduce more concrete and complete legislation to help Canadians who are 60 or over. [Text]

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GARNISHEES AGAINST CROWN

speakeroldname: Mr. E. F. Whelan (Essex South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GARNISHEES AGAINST CROWN
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-143, to amend the Financial Administration Act (discretionary garnishee against crown).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GARNISHEES AGAINST CROWN
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING GARNISHEES AGAINST CROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to remedy the grievance suffered by creditors who cannot collect their just debts from federal civil servants because the crown's certificate of employment is a certificate of protection against the garnishee of wages process of the courts.

More than 300 years ago the British House of Commons cleaned up a similar injury to the public caused by members who used their parliamentary privileges to protect their employees and servants against the debt processes of the courts. On November 28, 1661 the House of Commons passed the following resolution:
This house, taking into further debate the great grievances of the people occasioned by protections,
Resolves, that all protections, and written certificates of the members of this house, be declared void in law, and be forthwith withdrawn and called in, and that none be granted for the future. . . .
-and on January 31, 1781 the house amended the standing order to make it more effectual by adding a punishment:
and if any protection or written certificate shall be granted by any member, such member shall make satisfaction to the party injured, and shall be liable to the censure of the house.
For 304 years the treasury bench has sat on this example we members of the House of Commons set them. The government should now do what we did, either adopt this bill and wipe out this class privilege or, if it intends to perpetuate it, make satisfaction to the injured creditors.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

MEAT INSPECTION-BILINGUAL APPROVAL STAMPS
speechtext: Do the meat inspection services of the federal government now have bilingual stamps reading "Canada Approved" and "Qualite Canada" to be applied on meat carcasses in all slaughterhouses throughout Canada recognized by the Department of Agriculture and, if not, for what reason has this change not been made and, as it has been requested for over a year, when is it the intention to make it?

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Beer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MEAT INSPECTION-BILINGUAL APPROVAL STAMPS
speechtext:
The meat inspection service of the federal government does not

Questions
have bilingual stamps reading "Canada Approved" and "Qualite Canada." The Canada Department of Agriculture has been investigating actively a means of providing an inspection stamp or stamps which would adequately serve the two official languages.
There are two ways of providing for this. One is to have separate stamps or legends for the two languages. This approach, after careful investigation, has been rejected since it would in many instances require firms to maintain a double inventory of stamps and labels because certain importing countries of Canadian meat products require the inspection legend to be in English.
The other approach, which the department is now pursuing, is a single stamp or legend which would be bilingual in nature yet sufficiently concise as to retain the distinctive trade mark nature of the present stamp which has come to be widely recognized in Canada and internationally as the mark of Canadian veterinary meat inspection.
At the present time consideration is being given at the international level, through
O.E.C.D., to develop a common form of meat inspection stamp for use by member countries. It is desirable that the Canadian legend should conform as closely as possible to any recommendation which might be made by
O.E.C.D. and action with respect to a revised Canadian legend is being withheld in the meantime.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: MONEY LOST THROUGH CHEQUE TAMPERING
speechtext:
After encashment each cheque drawn on the Receiver General of Canada is reconciled to the amount in which it was originally issued, by the comptroller of the treasury. If the amount claimed by the encashing bank exceeds the amount for which the cheque was originally issued due to the cheque having been raised, settlement is made with the encashing bank for the original amount, the excess being a responsibility of the encashing bank. In addition, if evidence is produced that a bank has cashed a cheque on a forged endorsement, the amount involved is recovered from that bank.
In neither case is there any loss of public funds due to tampering with cheques.

INCIDENCE OF MONGOLISM DUE TO FLUORIDATION
speechtext:

2.	Has the same department been informed of Dr. I. Rapaport's recently published data relative to the mechanism by which fluoride could increase the incidence of Mongolism?
3.	Is the said department still of the opinion that no ill effect has ever been encountered after the use of "normally" fluoridated water?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCIDENCE OF MONGOLISM DUE TO FLUORIDATION
speechtext: The Department of National Health and Welfare has reviewed Dr. Rapaport's data relating to fluoridation in Wisconsin and its possible relationship to mongolism and has also consulted the United States public health service concerning this matter. On the basis of its findings this department regards Dr. Rapaport's data as unconvincing. At the present time the department is not aware of authentic evidence indicating that any ill effects have ever been encountered in North America by consumption of water fluoridated at one part per million. On the contrary, there are many reports in the scientific literature attesting to the safety and value of fluoridation as a public health measure.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF COASTGUARD SHIPS
ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF COASTGUARD SHIPS
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of Transport administrative control over the coastguard ships, Rally, Rapid and Relay?
2.	If so, what was the position of these ships at sea or in what port were they anchored on December 1, 1964?
3.	Was a directive issued to any of these ships by the proper government authority, to go to the rescue of the lobster boats Jenny and Judy near Cape Sable island, Nova Scotia?
4.	What efforts were made by the Canadian coastguard on December 1, 1964 to rescue Stillman Quinlam and James Smith when their engine failed in the boat Jenny and Judy and they were unable to return to port?
5.	Has the government given any consideration to constructing adequate ships for service in the Canadian coastguard capable of carrying out rescue operations in times of disaster?
6.	Will the government give consideration to amending the coastguard regulations so that captains of coastguard ships may be permitted to tow any disabled shipping to the nearest port?
7.	How many letters of complaint relative to the inefficiency of the existing Canadian coastguard have been received by the Department of Transport during 1964?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Charles Caniin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL OF COASTGUARD SHIPS
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2.	Rapid in Dartmouth having main engines repaired. Rally in Dartmouth having defective electronic equipment repaired. Relay had just returned to Saint John from patrol and was standing by for incidents in bay of Fundy area.
3.	No. Rapid and Rally were unserviceable. Relay was allocated to bay of Fundy operations as a vessel of her size could have achieved little in the exceptionally severe conditions that she would have encountered outside the bay.
4.	The nearest ships to the scene were the naval escorts Terra Nova and Gatineau. These were diverted to go and help but could not reach the area in time because of the very severe weather.
5.	All Canadian coastguard ships are capable of carrying out rescue operations in areas and weather conditions appropriate to their size. Much useful rescue work is continually being done. A number of coastguard ships are now being equipped with stabilizing devices

which will improve their capability for rescue in heavy weather. Design studies for other types are also underway.
6.	Coastguard ships can and do tow disabled craft when they are in genuine distress and when this is the best way of dealing with the emergency. The government does not have enough ships to provide a free towing service to every vessel which is broken down and is not in any danger or distress. In these circumstances, it is the normal seafaring practice for vessels to make their own arrangements with another craft or through commercial towing companies.
7.	No letters specifically complaining of coastguard inefficiency have been received in the minister's office, or by departmental officials during 1964.

speechtext: May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he would give the house an outline of the critical and perilous position in which the United Nations finds itself as a result of the motion moved or to be moved by the ambassador from Albania. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN POSITION ON PROPOSED MOTION RESPECTING NATIONS IN DEFAULT
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Greenwood gave me notice of his intention to ask a question along those lines. In answer to the right hon. gentleman I would say that if tomorrow there were a confrontation on article XIX as a result of the action taken by Albania, Canada would, of course, vote in favour of the application of article XIX. However, the government hopes that a confrontation can be avoided, and that if necessary an adjournment can be arranged to permit negotiations between the parties in financial default and the other members of the United Nations.
The assembly is to resume tomorrow. However, there may well be a further adjournment. Albania is the only country which is seeking to bring on a confrontation at this time. Albania itself is in default and would be affected by article XIX, as would the Soviet union.
I regret to say that the financial situation facing the United Nations continues to present the organization with a serious crisis. There is a reluctance on the part of the Soviet union and other countries to pay a sufficient amount of money to avoid the implications of article XIX.
Canada will continue, as she has in the past, to put forward solutions which may bring about a compromise, but I must say that all the solutions put forward by Canada and indeed by other countries have been, in this regrettable situation, unavailing to date.

tally grouped with terminal and western elevators licensed under the Canada Grain Act.
I realize that the measures in the bill now before the house make provision for (a) a minimum hourly wage of $1.25 for all employees 17 years of age or over, regardless of sex; (b) a standard work week of 40 hours or eight hours a day and (c) a maximum of eight hours overtime per employee per week with minimum pay for overtime calculated at one and a half times the regular hourly rate. It is in this regard that the difficulties of the mills and truckers arise. I understand that by special permission of the Minister of Labour some additional overtime may be permitted if need is proven to the satisfaction of the minister.
While the above listed measures may not appear on the surface to be overly restrictive or costly, full compliance would adversely affect levels of labour efficiency and add materially to operating costs. It has been brought to my attention by these smaller mills that opposition to enforced involvement under this legislation is not based on any wish or desire to restrict the earning power of employees of member firms.
The operation of an average feed mill or local grain elevator does not lend itself to shift work or the employment of casual labour at peak production periods or at times of seasonal pressures such as occur during harvesting seasons. Operational skills that are only gained through training and experience are required for successful plant performance and customer servicing. Key employees cannot be relieved by inexperienced labour during rush periods, nor can plants afford anything less than the fullest utilization of available manpower.
Largely situated in rural areas or in the less populated centres of the province, local feed mills and grain elevators are not required to compete with large industrial centres for their labour requirements. If forced to operate under the jurisdiction of the federal labour code, mills and elevators so situated will be automatically deprived of the opportunity to take advantage of labour pay rates that prevail locally for local help. It could be pointed out that the most unreasonable feature of the minister's ruling in this section of industry is that members of the local feed and grain trade are being placed under federal labour jurisdiction while unrelated business operations of a local character are subject only to provincial labour regulations.

Canada Labour Code
The second point that gives us some concern with regard to Bill No. C-126 is the trucking industry. Some of the proposals incorporated in the bill are detrimental to the truckers, as I am sure we all understand, and also of course to thousands of citizens moving household effects. This legislation, if enacted in its present form, would only result in a very considerable increase in operating costs which must eventually be passed on to the public at large, thus resulting in an increase in the cost of living.
I understand some of these household moving companies do a considerable amount of business with the Department of National Defence and other government departments in connection with the movement of government personnel, and any increase in the rates charged will inevitably fall upon the taxpayers. It is a well known fact that speed of transportation is a necessary factor in today's economy. If the bill is passed with trucking included, it will prolong the time taken by these truckers in moving from point to point with resulting inconvenience to the public.
In view of the foregoing points and to prevent the interprovincial trucking industry from bearing a burden which would be intolerable to say the least, I would ask the minister to consider taking the necessary steps to exempt the trucking industry from the provisions of Bill No. C-126 and also to exempt independent, local, retail feed mills. In closing may I tell the minister that I am in favour of the principle of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to speak at great length and create unnecessary delay in the passage of this bill. I should like to place on record that I am in agreement with its general purpose. However, when the bill was introduced I placed some questions to the minister concerning its application to the fishing industry, and in view of the many clauses in part I dealing with hours of work I believe these points should be clarified before the bill is passed.
As is stated in the title, this is a bill respecting hours of work, minimum wages, annual vacations and holidays with pay in federal works, undertakings and businesses, but it is somewhat difficult to determine exactly the meaning of federal businesses and undertakings.
Clause 3(l)(a) says the bill will apply to-
-any work, undertaking or business carried on for or in connection with navigation and shipping, whether inland or maritime, including the operation of ships and transportation by ship anywhere in Canada.
I ask the minister would this apply only to ships operated by the government, or does it apply to all Canadian owned ships operating within Canadian territorial waters? Does it apply to our coastal freighters as well as to ships operating between our provinces? Does it apply to our deep sea fishing fleet operating out of our coastal ports?
When I asked these questions on October 19 last year the minister, as recorded at page 9203 of Hansard, replied that the matter of trawlers operating out of a fish plant would ultimately be a question for the Canadian

courts to determine, and expressed the view that trawlers operating as part of a fish plant on shore would come under provincial jurisdiction. He also stated that already one fishermen's union had been certified under provincial labour legislation. I presume he was referring to a fishermen's union in British Columbia because to my knowledge there is no deep sea fishermen's union certified or functioning on the Atlantic coast.
In addition to this there are independent trawlers which function for the shore based fish plants and which operate under what might be called a gentlemen's agreement. What would be the position of these independent operators if this bill applies to their industry? In view of these facts I now ask the minister to make a clear statement on the application of the bill to the Canadian fishing industry, with particular emphasis on its application to our deep sea fishing fleet.
I know that as a fellow mariner he would not wish to have a bill passed by this parliament that would cause the operators of our deep sea trawlers to go to the courts in order to ascertain the legality of working irregular hours, sometimes 20 or more hours a day, which is standard for fishing crews when operating at sea and when they have a good catch of fish. Due to the perishable nature of the catch it is absolutely impossible to adopt regular hours of employment on a fishing dragger.
Normally a dragger is allowed 10 or 12 days at sea. At the end of that time it must return to port so that its catch can be processed and shipped to market in prime condition. While it is on the fishing banks storms can occur, and the actual catching of fish is at irregular hours. Anyone who has gone fishing knows a whole day may pass without a nibble and just as you start to go home the fish start to bite. The same applies in our deep sea fishing operations, and when the fish are running they must be cleaned and placed below decks regardless of the hours of work involved.
After reading the hours of work as defined on page 4 of the bill I say frankly to the minister that it will have disastrous effects on our fishing industry and the income of our fishermen if these provisions are applied to them. All of the men engaged in the fishing industry are naturally concerned about this bill.
Today we have a whaling industry on both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts, and the whaling ships operate with permanent employees. In addition to the actual fishermen there is
Canada Labour Code
another class of employees involved, the truck drivers who deliver the fish from the processing plants on the Atlantic coast to places in Quebec, Ontario and the United States market. These men are also vitally concerned about the application of the bill to their industry. It is not at all unusual to see large transport trucks leaving Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, at seven or eight o'clock at night, or on a Sunday, following the landing of a large catch of fish which is perishable and which must be quickly transported to market.
The truck drivers are willing to work irregular hours, and long hours, because the transportation of fish provides them with steady employment. The very nature of the business would not permit unnecessary delays imposed as a result of the provisions of this bill. I hope the minister will answer some of these questions which are disturbing people in the fishing industry.
One final criticism I have to make of the bill is that it is almost wide open in its application and vests too much authority in the minister. One of the two amendments he has mentioned deals with the transitional provisions and deferments which may be granted by the minister if he is satisfied they are necessary; but on reading the entire bill it can be seen final authority always rests with the minister. If this be necessary then it is good that the minister is a representative from Nova Scotia, but this is just one more instance of the growing bureaucracy and red tape woven around the Canadian people by this government. It is the further concentration of power in the hands of a few people-

I wish to make a few comments with respect to this clause. A good deal was said during the latter part of last evening with regard to the trucking industry, and more has been said today. I believe it should be pointed out that the amendment to clause 51 and the averaging provisions in clause 5 are sufficiently wide in scope to deal with the objections which the trucking industry has raised. The averaging provisions allow some 400 hours for a steady year of employ-

Canada Labour Code
ment. This is provided without there being any necessity for an amendment to the bill.
Then again, the provisions of the proposed amendment permit the minister to defer the application of the restriction on hours in the case of any particular industry for a period of 18 months. The amendment goes on to provide that this period may be further extended as a result of the findings of an inquiry which may be set up, should the inquiry determine that a longer period of deferment, or suspension, is necessary on the grounds that an industry was unduly disturbed by the terms of the legislation. So, the trucking industry has the 400 hour leeway provided by the bill. It is entitled to apply for an extension of 18 months and, in addition, if it can be shown that the application of this measure has caused undue dislocation, it can secure a further extension of the period mentioned. Machinery exists under the Inquiries Act for full investigation.
In these circumstances it is difficult for me to understand how much further we could go in labour legislation in order to satisfy any particular group which was dissatisfied with the bill, without exempting that group entirely from its provisions-and I do not believe it would be the desire of any hon. member that the trucking industry should be exempted from the provisions of this bill. We all know there is a legitimate grievance inasmuch as those truckers who operate inter-provincially would be placed in unfair competition with others whose operations are carried on exclusively within the boundaries of one province. But the averaging provision and, in particular, the provisions for deferment to which I have called attention could conceivably allow them an indefinite period in which to comply with the requirements of the bill, and in these circumstances I do not believe there ought to be any strong objection from the trucking industry.
In the additional time available, provincial legislatures could set standards for intraprovincial truckers to comply with minimum requirements similar to those set out in the bill before us. The net result undoubtedly will be the enactment of provincial legislation setting standards similar to those which are contained in the bill before us. As a result, the interprovincial truckers will not be in unfair competition with their competitors.
A good deal has been said during this discussion about the objections of the trucking industry and the steps which have been taken to meet those objections. We have heard little, if anything, about the advantages which will
[Mr. Munro.l
ultimately accrue to the industry when uniform legislation exists throughout the country applying to truckers under both federal and provincial jurisdiction. The latter will ultimately, I am sure, have the benefit of minimum standards similar to those now to be enacted. This will come about as a result of the pressure which will be brought to bear on provincial legislatures not only by the truckers themselves but by ordinary common sense.
I should like to refer to a brief submitted by the international brotherhood of teamsters. This document called attention to some of the hazards which are ever present in the life of a transport driver because of failure to limit hours of work. The brief tells us how in many cases such men have lost their lives on the highway in accidents caused by fatigue due to long hours spent at the wheel, or by the use of pep pills to stay awake. Sometimes the reactions of drivers are adversely affected by the taking of these pills in order to complete a haul over long distances under pressure of time.
I believe the committee would be interested in the findings of an Ontario magistrate. The case I have in mind is an example of the serious accidents which can be caused by driver fatigue. The magistrate is referring to a fatal accident which took place on June 19, 1964; he felt it served to highlight the entire problem which truck drivers face. Four members of an Ottawa family were killed in a flaming head-on crash with a truck on highway 69 near Pointe au Baril. The truck driver suffered severe burns. The impact exploded 100 gallons of gasoline in the truck. Perhaps I could read at this point from the document before me.
When the case came to court, the crown maintained that the reason the truck driver was travelling in the wrong lane and tailed to avoid collision was because he had gone to sleep at the wheel. Stressing the laws covering dangerous driving, the crown cited other cases of drivers becoming drowsy due to excessive hours on the road and thus being guilty of driving in a manner dangerous to the public.
Magistrate F.C. Powell who tried the case in Parry Sound had this to say in his summation:
There is ample evidence to show that the defendant who had been working and driving for the greater part of 30 hours prior to the collision with very little if any sleep, and driving over 500 miles in that period, knew or should have known, as he said to Mr. Wing (crown witness) that he should have pulled off the road and had a sleep. Therefore, I find that the collision was caused by the defendant going to sleep when he needed rest and thus allowing his truck to travel on a course into the path of the northbound Vauxhall. This amounts to driving dangerously-

Then he went on to say when he was imposing sentence, showing his understanding of the problem:
In the first place, the offence that you have committed-
He is referring in this particular case to the fault on the part of the truck driver:
-requires that the court impose a penalty which will be a deterrent to others who would run the risk of falling asleep while driving a motor vehicle. In my mind, to drive while you are overtired and knowing that you need sleep is Just as bad as driving while you are impaired by alcohol.
Then he says:
This must be a deterrent which is especially important to truck drivers generally who would drive their vehicles under such conditions. The majority of truck operators have set hours for their drivers.
Then he goes on with this important comment:
I realize that independent drivers are allowed to operate regardless of how many hours they are on the road and this should be discouraged because it is something which is a hazard to the general public using the highway.
In most provinces of this country there is no limitation on the hours a transport driver drives his truck. In Ontario I understand there is a limitation of 60 hours, which has never had any history of enforcement. I am only pointing this out, Mr. Chairman, because we have heard one side and surely we should hear the other side, which involves the many employees in the trucking industry. I cannot help but feel that the provisions of this legislation, even though they may not apply now, as I say, may be an encouragement to all the provincial legislatures across this country to impose similar legislation so that we will have an end to the excessive hours that drivers of transports are driving on the highway, causing death to others in many cases, a danger to other citizens on the highway and, last but not least, involving many of them who have a history of overwork over a period of 10 or 15 years, winding up being burned out and having to find other employment.
Therefore I would hope the committee would feel that the hours of work provisions in this particular bill, when considered in conjunction with the averaging provisions of the proposed amendment to clause 51, are ample to deal with the objections of the trucking industry and have taken their viewpoint into account. I would therefore hope that the committee would let the clause pass.

The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg did make some reference to the situation which exists in the province of British Columbia, from which I come. Many of our coastal vessels come under federal labour jurisdiction, but my understanding is that the basic work pattern which has been established as a result of union negotiations both in respect of the fishing industry under provincial jurisdiction and the fishing industry under federal jurisdiction, as well as in fields of operations such as our coastal tow boats, is a pattern which does conform to the principle of the eight hour day and 40 hour week. This is particularly true when one takes into account the arrangement for averaging the hours of work over an appropriate period of time.
If conditions in the maritime fishing industry are such that any member of this house is concerned that the rather modest proposals with regard to the limitation of hours of work set forth in the bill as minimum standards will have a bad effect upon the operation of that industry, I suggest there are other steps that should be taken to correct the situation, rather than allowing a

situation to continue which makes it difficult for the industry to operate under the proposals of the bill if one takes into account the suggestion that the principle of averaging be applied in an appropriate manner. So I am dealing with clause 5 but, as I say, I cannot do so intelligently without some regard to what the minister said yesterday. This brings me immediately, of course, to what the minister did say and what is proposed in the amendments, because only through an interpretation of them am I in a position to express my views on clause
5.
Some of my colleagues have made reference already to the question of ministerial discretion. I cannot deal with that without reference to clause 3 of the bill. This clause, which has already been considered, refers to the legislation applying to "any work, undertaking or business". I call the attention of the committee to the fact that the words used there are in the singular, "work, undertaking or business", and as I construe the clause it would appear that clause 5 and clause 51 could be applied to any single business which is federal in nature. Consequently one can contemplate a situation where the rigid operation of clause 5 with regard to a number of businesses might be subject to applications under clause 51 by any one of those businesses or works or undertakings for suspension, deferment or outright cancellation of the application of clause 5. This, of course, does give me great anxiety, as I am sure it does the minister who, if this legislation goes through in its present form, will have all these difficult and worrisome problems deposited on his doorstep. He will have to exercise his discretion in respect of these issues.
Under the proposed clause 51 the minister may by order-I emphasize the word "may" -defer or suspend the operation of part I in respect of any federal work or undertaking. He can do so where it has been established to his satisfaction, as I take it, that the application of clause 5 would be or is unduly prejudicial to the interests of the employees, or would be or is seriously detrimental to the operation of the federal work, undertaking or business. I am concerned in this respect. The minister having had it established to his satisfaction that such is the case, does the use of the word "may" mean that the minister still has a choice? Once it has been established to his satisfaction within the meaning of paragraph (a) or (b) of subclause 1 of clause 51, can the minister still exercise his discretion? Does the word "may" mean that he can

reject his own findings and refuse to defer or suspend the operation of part I with regard to a particular business or undertaking or is it that the word "may" must be interpreted in the sense that it means "shall"? These words are interchangeable. Once the minister has found to his satisfaction that these conditions exist, must he make this order of deferment or suspension? I think the minister should tell us now because on his answer may depend our views as to what he should do with regard to clause 5.
I pass on to the next part of the proposed new clause 51 which provides that a longer period of deferment or suspension or, indeed, the actual rejection of the operation of that entire part of the act may be provided in the case of a business or undertaking after an inquiry has been held under clause 35. Again the word used there is "may". I am assuming that a situation might arise where an inquiry has been held. A work, or undertaking or industry has appeared and made representations in the inquiry to the commissioner named under the Inquiries Act, has established certain facts and the result of the inquiry has been a finding-it would be an absolute finding of fact by the commissioner within section 51(2). Under those circumstances is there still a discretion left to the minister? May he refuse to accept the finding of the inquiry, or is he compelled to accept and make the recommendation to the governor in council, which in turn is compelled to issue the order?
I think this is tremendously important because it means that a vested right may accrue to the business, to the undertaking or the venture, on the finding by the inquiry, and the refusal of the minister or governor in council to order might give to the business the right to compel, through mandamus or otherwise, that the finding be followed.
I believe we should hear from the minister before passing clause 5. We should know his view as to whether he would be compelled to follow this finding by the commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the last subclause of the proposed clause 51, as suggested by the minister, is to the effect that the governor in council upon the recommendation of the minister, with or without an inquiry pursuant to clause 55, may by order vary and exempt from time to time any order made under subclause 2.
I can envision a situation where a dozen individual businesses might apply for exemption, following which there would be an in-

quiry under clause 35, with respect to some of them. An order in council may be passed exempting them from the provisions of this legislation. If I construe subclause 5 under its literal sense it means the minister may then, without any inquiry, remove from any of those businesses the suspension or cancellation which was granted to them. This is a very invidious situation.
I would certainly like to feel that before passing clause 5 we shall hear from the minister as to whether or not in his opinion the removal of any cancellation under subclause 5 will only take place following an inquiry. If not, what are the reasons he sees fit to give to the committee for clause 5 being left as it is?
Finally, the same wording applies. The word there is "may." The minister still has the ministerial discretion despite any finding that may be made.
I am not trying to be difficult or technical. I am just trying to look ahead to a number of situations that are bound to arise. In view of the fact that over a period of three months since the legislation was last before the committee all these problems have arisen and been brought to the attention of the minister and other members of the committee, it indicates the dangers which may lie ahead if this legislation is pursued without the most careful examination. I have heard from a great many industries. I am not going to pursue an argument in that connection because all the arguments have been well made by my colleagues on this side of the chamber. However, I invite the minister to reply to these questions I have raised and I would hope we might have an opportunity, after hearing his reply, of suggesting what in our views might be more suitable wording for clause 51, to add to what he suggested in his speech last night.

Maybe the time is long overdue for me to make some remarks in an attempt to deal with a number of important questions which have been raised so far in our discussion. May I begin by turning to a number of specific questions which were put

to me by the hon. member for Ontario, questions which were to some extent repeated by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce today.
The hon. member for Ontario asked me how many industries had made representations to me in connection with Bill C-126. I have received a large number of delegations and read a large number of briefs, besides travelling in various parts of the country in an effort to appreciate the problems of the principal industries which have expressed concern about the application of this measure. These industries are: Trucking, railways, shipping, stevedoring, the handling of grain in elevators, fishing and feed mill operation. Other industries under federal jurisdiction have come forward but it is these, the ones I have just mentioned, which have expressed the greatest intensity of concern about the application of these provisions, especially the provision relating to hours of work.
The committee should bear in mind that a bill of this kind is bound to effect changes. If it were not intended to effect changes it would be useless. Please do not ask me not to interfere with the status quo, as was done last night, because that is the purpose of this measure. If we do not believe in making changes we ought not to have given support to this bill on second reading. I have been asked whether my amendments have been approved by the industries affected. Well, of course not, because my first obligation is to present these amendments to the committee and not to secure prior approval from industries which have a legitimate interest, in the provisions of this bill.
But I did-and the house is aware of this -issue a statement on November 5 last, in a press release, indicating in a general way what changes generally might be affected to meet the particular requirements of the trucking industry.
I believe it is safe and fair to say that, while the trucking industry, understandably, would be much happier if they were completely removed from the bill, the number, frequency and vigour of the representations have decreased since this statement was made last November. I realize that the trucking industry has special problems. The hours of work in the trucking industry are, in my opinion, excessive; they ought to be reduced for health and safety reasons and in order to meet more closely the general hours that prevail in the industry. I realize, as well, that this desirable objective ought to be undertaken with the least possible disruption of the operations of this important industry 20220-725
Canada Labour Code
and with the least possible effect on the welfare of the employees concerned.
The principal problem that makes the exercise of federal jurisdiction so difficult and necessitates a time for adjustment is the fact of divided jurisdiction. If we imposed on July 1, 1965, the standard hours of work on the trucking industry there would undoubtedly be very serious effects. Our standards are higher than the provincial standards and are higher than the standards prevailing in the United States. We would be putting the truckers under federal jurisdiction at a considerable competitive disadvantage compared with those operating under these different standards. That is part of the problem.
Another part of the problem is the irregularity of the hours. Sometimes the truckers must make long runs involving 10 or 12 hours on the road which, if the bill were strictly observed, it would be impossible to do. We have two provisions which I want to mention -there are others, of course-relating to trucking especially that can be applied to that industry and to other industries. There is the question of averaging. Clause 5 says:
Where the nature of the work In an industrial establishment necessitates irregular distribution of an employee's hours of work, the hours of work in a day and the hours of work in a week may be calculated, in such manner and in such circumstances as may be prescribed by the regulations, as an average for a period of two or more weeks.
I have stated that the "two or more weeks" comprehends a period as long as a full year. That possibility exists where there is an irregular distribution of an employee's hours of work. This would mean that through an averaging provision an employee could work 2,080 hours on the average in a year without overtime provisions coming into effect, and that an additional 416 hours would apply at overtime rates before the maximum hours in the total year would apply. This provides an opportunity for the trucking industry to average; it provides an opportunity for the grain elevators to average-and this is, in my judgment, an almost complete answer to their problems-over a period of a full year to take into account the seasonal peaks of harvest and the slack periods.
I have a good deal of evidence that I could put before the committee that supports my conclusion that the case of the grain elevators can be adequately dealt with through the system of averaging in so far as hours are concerned. The grain elevators have not complained about the other aspects of the bill. This averaging can apply to the trucking in-

Canada Labour Code
dustry. What further provisions have we made? We had the trucking industry, among other industries, in mind when we drafted the original clause 51, which provides that upon its being submitted that the immediate imposition of these hours would prejudice the welfare of the employees or the operation of the industrial establishment-and later I shall say why in my judgment it was desirable to have the minister and the governor in council do this rather than another body, subject of course to the views of the committee-the minister may defer or suspend the application of the hours of work section for a period of 18 months.
I am satisfied that the facts that have been put forward by the trucking industry are sound and that this industry would be among the most eligible for a deferment for that period. In that case we would immediately establish an inquiry under clause 35. I listened with interest to some of the proposals as to the best type of inquiry that ought to be set up, but surely the inquiry ought to be by a person or persons of independence and fairmindedness who would hear the views of employees and employers with respect to an appropriate regime of hours. After this hearing they would make their recommendations, and on the basis of those recommendations the minister would be able to recommend to the cabinet, to the governor in council, an appropriate regime of hours that would apply beyond that 18 month period. Surely this meets the problem of flexibility with respect to this industry and other industries.
The hon. member for Ontario referred to a statement which I had made suggesting that all the provinces meet with the federal government with a view to developing common standards for the trucking industry. That is the ultimate solution. If we do nothing in this industry we will never get common standards. But the ultimate solution to this problem is to work toward a system of common standards, co-operatively with the provinces, that would apply to trucking under federal and provincial jurisdiction.

This flows from section 45 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and my hon. friend will realize also that grain elevators do come under this particular bill because they have been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada, under the Canada Grain Act. Federal labour legislation does include all works that have been declared for the general advantage of Canada.
My hon. friend has raised some problems in connection with feed mills and the hours of work provisions, which is presumably a matter of concern to the local feed mills. I have already explained the application of clause 51 and the averaging provision which apply according to their own terms. Clause 51 comes into effect when it can be demonstrated that the imposition of these hours of work will create hardship either on the operation or on the employees within the operation.
Perhaps I might draw my hon. friend's attention to another provision of the bill which provides an opportunity to defer the application of the $1.25 per hour provision for a period of 18 months, only in respect of local enterprises, and it is very restrictive for that period of time. I do hope that hon. members of this committee will not put forward the argument that after that period of time $1.25 per hour is an inappropriate wage even for feed mills in local areas of any part of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, earlier this afternoon I asked some specific questions relating to the application of this bill to the Canadian fishing industry, and I should like to know whether the minister is in a position to provide answers to those questions.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am
pleased to provide the hon. member with answers.
On October 19 the hon. member asked a question as to the coverage of this bill in respect of the fishing industry. The short answer is that the fishing industry is within the scope of the bill but, because of the terms of the bill, it will have very little significance for the fishing industry.
The constitutional position is that parliament has exclusive authority to legislate in relation to seacoast and inland fisheries under section 91 (12) of the B.N.A. Act of 1867. The expression "fisheries" must comprehend the activity of "fishing". The fishing industry is concerned with that activity and, as such, is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of parliament. Bill C-126 applies, by its terms, to employers and employees engaged upon or in connection with the operation of any works, undertakings or businesses within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of parliament, and to employment therein. The bill would therefore apply to the inland and seacoast fishing industries.
Canada Labour Code
Persons employed in the operation of a fishing vessel may be employed in the capacity of seamen or fishermen, or both. As seamen, the bill would apply to them as a matter relating to navigation and shipping. I think that is clear enough. As fishermen engaged in fisheries, the bill would have application for the reasons already given.
However, the bill applies only where there is an employer and an employee, and most fishermen are engaged in a "joint adventure" by a sharing or partnership agreement, or fish on their own. Because of the sharing or joint adventure aspect, or because of the self-employment character of the situation, as far as we can determine only a small number of fishermen work for wages and would come under the provisions of this bill. The greater number of fishermen engaged in the fishing industry are excluded because of the arrangements under which they work in the industry-not as employees, but as self-employed persons or persons engaged in a joint adventure.

The only question I asked last evening was with regard to some indication
from the minister as to what is work. 1 pointed out that there is no reference to that in the definition clause of the bill and that it is a matter of practical concern to employees in some segments of industry under federal jurisdiction. Can the minister give us an indication of what he has in mind in relation to the interpretation of the word "work"?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: The terms "working hours" and "to work" in clause 5 (1) are not defined in the bill, nor is there any provision for defining them by regulation. They therefore have the meaning commonly assigned to these words. We consider this to be the hours during which an employee works for an employer or, at the direction of the employer, is present and available for work at the work place. As the hon. member will have realized from my preceding statement, we consider that any attempt at definition might be more restrictive than helpful in carrying out the purposes of the legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: That explanation is a very interesting one. Can the minister give us his understanding of how this will apply to air line employees whom I specifically mentioned? subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: The employee is at work when he is at the disposal of the employer and under his direction at the place of work.
